title: The Names of God
subtitle: Part 1 · How God makes Himself known in the Old Testament

sections.title: Why God’s names matter
sections.subtitle: A name is a revelation, not a label

blocks.text:
In the Bible a name is more than a tag. It says who someone is, what they have done, or what they will do. When God gives a name for Himself, or when someone who has met Him gives Him one, it is a small window into His character.

That is why Scripture talks about God’s *name* the way it does: people call on it (Gen 4:26), trust in it (Ps 20:7), run into it for safety (Prov 18:10), and Jesus teaches us to pray that it be hallowed (Matt 6:9).

God is not a puzzle we solve by collecting His titles. But each name was given at a real moment, usually to real people in real trouble, and each one tells us something He wanted known.

**Three things to know before we start:**

1. **LORD, Lord and GOD.** When your English Bible prints **LORD** in small capitals, the Hebrew is God’s personal name, YHWH. When it prints **Lord**, the Hebrew is usually *Adonai*, “Lord, Master.” When it prints **GOD** in capitals, it is YHWH again, where *Adonai* sits right next to it (“Lord GOD”), so the translators avoided writing “Lord LORD.”
2. **Many “compound names” began as place or altar names.** *YHWH Yireh*, *YHWH Nissi*, *YHWH Shalom* and *YHWH Shammah* were names given to a mountain, two altars and a city. They are still true statements about God, and that is how the church has used them, but it is honest to say where they came from.
3. **Some meanings are debated.** Where scholars genuinely disagree (El Shaddai is the big one), this lesson says so rather than picking the most inspiring option.
What name or title for God do you use most when you pray? Why that one?
Can you think of a time when you understood something about God only because of what you were going through?

Opening idea: ask the group what their own name means and whether it fits them. Then point out that God’s names always fit, because He either chose them or confirmed them.

The LORD/Lord/GOD typography explanation is worth slowing down for. Most people have never noticed it, and it changes how they read the Old Testament for the rest of their lives. Have them open to Gen 15:2 or Ps 110:1 and look at the capitals.

blocks.note: God; the mighty one. Plural in form, used with singular verbs for the one true God

blocks.text:
**Elohim** is the first name for God in the Bible and one of the most common, appearing roughly 2,600 times. It is the general Hebrew word for God, and it is what the opening chapter uses thirty-odd times as God speaks, makes, separates, sees, names and blesses.

The word is **plural in form** (the *-im* ending), yet when it refers to the true God it almost always takes a **singular verb**. In Gen 1:1 “God *created*” is singular. Most Hebrew scholars explain this as a *plural of majesty or fullness*: God is so great that an ordinary singular word cannot hold Him.

Many Christians have also seen a hint of the Trinity here, especially with “Let **us** make man in **our** image” (Gen 1:26). Be careful: the plural ending alone does not prove the Trinity (the same word is used for a single pagan god like Dagon in Judg 16:23). But the Old Testament does leave room for plurality within the one God, and the New Testament fills that room in (John 1:1-3; Col 1:16).

Because *elohim* is a general word, the Bible also uses it for false gods (Exod 20:3, “no other *elohim*”), and occasionally for angels or human judges (Ps 82:6, which Jesus quotes in John 10:34). Context decides.

**What the name teaches:** God is the Creator, the one with power and authority over everything that exists, and He was there before anything else.

**In Christ:** “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). The Creator God of Genesis 1 is the Word who became flesh.
Elohim is the name used while God is creating. What does it mean for you personally that the God you pray to is the Creator?
Read Gen 1:26-27 again. What does it mean to be made in God’s image?

Be honest about the “plural = Trinity” argument. It is popular but weak on its own. Better to say: Gen 1:26 and the plural form are consistent with the Trinity and become meaningful in light of the New Testament.

Possible illustration: when the Queen used “we” she wasn’t claiming to be several people; that is roughly the plural of majesty.

blocks.note: God, mighty one; the oldest and simplest Semitic word for a god

blocks.text:
**El** is the short, singular word for God. It was the common word for a deity across the ancient Near East, and the Canaanites even had a chief god called El. Israel did not borrow that god; it used the ordinary word and filled it with the character of the one true God.

On its own *El* appears a little over 200 times, but its real importance is that it is the base of many of God’s names: **El Elyon**, **El Roi**, **El Shaddai**, **El Olam**, **El Qanna**, **El Chai**. It also shows up in hundreds of personal names: Isra-**el**, Dani-**el**, Samu-**el**, **El**ijah, Micha-**el**, Imman-u-**el**.

Look closely at Isaiah 9:6. One of the titles of the child who is to be born is **El Gibbor**, “Mighty God.” Isaiah uses the very same title for the LORD Himself in the next chapter (Isa 10:21). The prophet is saying the coming son of David will be God.

And Isaiah 7:14 promises **Immanu-El**, “God with us,” which Matthew applies directly to Jesus (Matt 1:23).
Many Bible names contain *El*. Why do you think parents gave their children names that said something about God?
Isaiah calls the coming child “Mighty God.” How does that change the way you read the Christmas story?

Fun group exercise: have people call out Bible names ending or starting in “el” and guess what they mean. Daniel = God is my judge; Samuel = heard by God (probably); Elijah = my God is Yah; Michael = who is like God?

blocks.note: The LORD; God’s personal, covenant name

blocks.text:
This is God’s own **personal name**, the name He gives Moses at the burning bush. It appears about 6,800 times, far more than any other name for God. Whenever you see **LORD** in capitals, this is the word underneath.

The four Hebrew letters (Y-H-W-H, sometimes called the *Tetragrammaton*) are related to the verb “to be.” God explains His name by saying “I AM WHO I AM” (next section). It is the name of the God who **is**, who is **present**, and who keeps His **covenant** promises.

**How is it pronounced?** Honestly, we are not certain. Over time Jews stopped saying the name aloud out of reverence and read *Adonai* (“Lord”) instead. Centuries later, scribes wrote the vowels of *Adonai* under the letters YHWH as a reminder to say “Lord.” English readers who combined those vowels with the consonants produced **“Jehovah,”** a form that never existed in ancient Hebrew. Most scholars think it was originally pronounced something like **Yahweh**, but that is a reconstruction.

This is also why the Greek Old Testament, and then the New Testament, translates YHWH as *Kyrios*, “Lord.” That matters, as we will see.

**A puzzle in Exodus 6:3.** God says He appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai, “but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.” Yet the name LORD is used all through Genesis. The most likely meaning is that they *knew the name* but had not yet *experienced what it meant*: the LORD who redeems His people and keeps His covenant in action. The exodus is where they would learn it.

When God later “proclaims the name of the LORD” to Moses (Exod 34:5-7), He doesn’t give a definition; He describes His character: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, forgiving, and just. That is what the name means.

**In Christ:** The New Testament writers take Old Testament verses about YHWH and apply them to Jesus. “Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” (Joel 2:32) becomes a promise about calling on Jesus (Rom 10:9-13). Isaiah 45:23, where YHWH says every knee will bow to Him, is applied to Jesus in Phil 2:9-11, who is given “the name that is above every name.”
God revealed His personal name to slaves in Egypt before He rescued them. What does it say about Him that He wants to be known personally, not just as “God”?
Read Exodus 34:6-7. Which part of God’s description of Himself do you most need to hear right now?
Why is it significant that Paul applies a YHWH passage from Isaiah to Jesus in Philippians 2?

This is the heart of the lesson. If time is short, cut elsewhere and keep this.

On “Jehovah”: say it gently. Many people love the hymns and the old usage. The point isn’t that it’s wrong to say, just that it’s a later English form.

Jehovah’s Witnesses make a lot of the name. If that comes up: the NT never uses YHWH; it consistently uses Kyrios, and applies Kyrios passages to Jesus. That is the stronger point.

blocks.note: to be, to become, to happen. The root behind God’s name

blocks.text:
Moses asks, in effect, “Who should I say sent me?” God answers: **“I AM WHO I AM”** (*ehyeh asher ehyeh*). The phrase can also be translated **“I will be who I will be.”** Both are true to the Hebrew, and both matter:

- **I AM:** God simply *is*. He depends on nothing, was made by no one, and is not defined by anyone else.
- **I WILL BE:** God is going to show who He is by what He does. Moses will find out by watching Him act.

Right before this, God had promised Moses, “I will be with you” (Exod 3:12), using the same verb, *ehyeh*. The God who IS, is the God who is **with** His people.

**In Christ:** Jesus deliberately uses this language. “Before Abraham was, **I am**” (John 8:58), and the crowd picks up stones, because they understood exactly what He was claiming. In John 18:5-6, when the soldiers come to arrest Him, Jesus says “I am he” (literally “I am”), and they draw back and fall to the ground.

John also records seven “I am” sayings with a picture attached: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way the truth and the life, the true vine.
Which translation speaks to you more right now: “I AM who I AM” or “I WILL BE who I will be”? Why?
Why did the crowd try to stone Jesus in John 8:58? What does that tell us about who He claimed to be?

Good place to list the seven “I am” sayings on a board. Ask which one people find most personal.

Note: in John 18:6 most English Bibles add “he,” but the Greek is just “I am” (ego eimi).

sections.title: Yah
sections.subtitle: The short form of the name, inside every Hallelujah

blocks.note: Yah; a shortened, poetic form of YHWH

blocks.text:
**Yah** is a short form of God’s name, used about 50 times, mostly in songs and psalms. The KJV prints it as “JAH” in Ps 68:4. It first appears in the song Moses and Israel sing after crossing the Red Sea.

You say it every time you say **Hallelujah**: *hallelu* (“praise!”) + *Yah*. So “Hallelujah” literally means “Praise the LORD!” It also appears in many names: Eli**jah** (“my God is Yah”), Isa**iah** (“Yah saves”), Jerem**iah**, Zechar**iah** (“Yah remembers”), Obad**iah** (“servant of Yah”).

**In Christ:** The name **Jesus** is the Greek form of the Hebrew *Yehoshua* (Joshua), “the LORD saves.” That is exactly why the angel says, “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt 1:21). The name of God is in the name of Jesus.
Knowing that “Hallelujah” means “Praise Yah,” how might that change the way you sing or say it?
The first “Yah” comes in a song right after a rescue (Exod 15). What has God rescued you from that deserves a song?
Short section. Good breather after the heavy YHWH material. Could sing a Hallelujah chorus or read Psalm 150 together.

blocks.note: Lord, my Lord; used only of God

blocks.text:
**Adonai** means “Lord” or “my Lord,” in the sense of master or owner. The ordinary word *adon* is used for human masters and husbands, but this special form, **Adonai**, is reserved for God. It appears about 440 times.

The first time anyone speaks to God this way is Abram in Genesis 15:2: “**O Lord GOD** (*Adonai YHWH*), what will you give me?” Abram calls God Master in the same breath as he honestly admits his disappointment. Calling God Lord doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine.

Isaiah sees **Adonai** “sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isa 6:1), and responds, “Here I am! Send me” (Isa 6:8). If He is Master, I am His servant.

**A careful note on Psalm 110:1.** “The LORD says to my Lord.” The first is YHWH. The second is *adoni*, “my lord,” the ordinary word normally used for a human master, not *Adonai*. Jesus uses this verse to ask how David’s son can also be David’s lord (Matt 22:41-46). The argument works because David, the king, calls this coming figure his superior.

**In Christ:** The earliest Christian confession was simply “**Jesus is Lord**” (Rom 10:9; 1 Cor 12:3). Given that Jews read “Lord” in place of God’s name, that was an astonishing thing for a Jew to say about a man.
Abram called God “Master” while telling Him honestly what he was disappointed about. Do you feel free to do both?
What would change this week if you treated Jesus as Master in one specific area of life?
Check the Ps 110 detail before teaching: many books say both words are “Adonai.” They aren’t; the Masoretic text has adoni in Ps 110:1. Worth getting right.

blocks.note: Most High; the one above all others

blocks.text:
**El Elyon** means “God Most High.” *Elyon* means upper or highest. The name first appears in one of the most mysterious scenes in Genesis: Abram returns from rescuing Lot, and **Melchizedek**, king of Salem and “priest of God Most High,” brings out bread and wine and blesses him.

Notice what Abram does in verse 22: he swears by “**the LORD, God Most High**.” He identifies the God Melchizedek worships with YHWH. There is only one Most High, and He is the LORD.

The name stresses God’s **supremacy**: He is above every king, nation and so-called god. It is a favourite name in the Psalms (Ps 91:1) and in Daniel, where even the pagan king Nebuchadnezzar finally confesses that “the Most High rules the kingdom of men” (Dan 4:17, 34).

**In Christ:** The angel tells Mary her son “will be called the **Son of the Most High**” (Luke 1:32). And Hebrews 7 says Jesus is a priest “after the order of Melchizedek” — a priest-king who blesses God’s people, forever.
Abram has just won a battle when he meets God Most High. Why might that be exactly the moment he needed to remember who is truly highest?
Psalm 91:1 talks about dwelling “in the shelter of the Most High.” What does dwelling there look like on an ordinary day?

Don’t get pulled into speculation about who Melchizedek “really” was (pre-incarnate Christ, Shem, etc.). Hebrews uses him as a type; Genesis tells us very little. Keep the focus on the name.

Note 2 verses later (14:23): Abram refuses the king of Sodom’s wealth. Knowing God Most High freed him from needing it.

blocks.note: seeing, sight; “a God of seeing”

blocks.text:
This name comes from **Hagar**, an Egyptian slave, pregnant, mistreated by Sarai, and running away into the wilderness. The angel of the LORD finds her by a spring, calls her by name, and asks two questions that go to the heart: “Where have you come from and where are you going?”

She responds by giving God a name: **“You are El Roi,”** “a God of seeing,” for she says, “Truly here I have seen him who looks after me.” The well was then called *Beer-lahai-roi*, “the well of the Living One who sees me.”

Think about who gives God this name. Not Abram, not a priest, not a prophet, but a foreign slave woman whom everyone else in the story uses and ignores. She is the first person in Scripture to give God a name.

God sees her again in Genesis 21:17-19, when she and Ishmael are dying of thirst, and He opens her eyes to a well.

**In Christ:** Jesus repeatedly *sees* people no one else sees: Nathanael under the fig tree (John 1:48), Zacchaeus in the tree (Luke 19:5), the widow putting in two coins (Mark 12:41-44), a woman at a well at noon (John 4). And He sees with compassion: “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them” (Matt 9:36). Hebrews says nothing is hidden from His sight, yet He sympathises with our weakness (Heb 4:13-15).
Hagar was on the run when God found her. Where are you most tempted to feel unseen?
Being seen by God can feel comforting or frightening. Which is it for you, and why? How does Heb 4:15-16 help?
Who around you is a “Hagar”: overlooked, used, or on the edge? How could you see them this week?

This one tends to hit people emotionally. Leave silence after reading Gen 16.

The angel also tells her to go back (16:9), which is hard. Be honest about that if someone raises it; God doesn’t remove all her hardship, but He promises a future for her son (16:10-12) and keeps seeing her (Gen 21).

blocks.note: Shaddai; traditionally “Almighty”

blocks.text:
**El Shaddai** is the name God uses when He appears to Abram at ninety-nine years old, with no son by Sarai, and renews the covenant: “I am **God Almighty**; walk before me, and be blameless” (Gen 17:1). He then promises a child to a couple long past having children.

*Shaddai* appears 48 times, especially in Genesis (with the patriarchs) and in **Job** (31 times), where the question is whether the Almighty can be trusted when life falls apart.

**What does Shaddai actually mean? Honestly, no one is sure.** The main options:

- **“Almighty.”** The traditional meaning, going back to the ancient Greek and Latin translations. This is what most English Bibles use.
- **“God of the mountain(s),”** from a related Akkadian word. The God who is strong, high and immovable.
- **“The one who is sufficient,”** from an old Jewish reading *she-dai*, “who is enough.”
- **“The many-breasted / nourishing one,”** from *shad*, “breast.” You’ll hear this one in sermons. Genesis 49:25 does put “Shaddai” beside “blessings of the breasts and of the womb,” but most scholars think this is wordplay rather than the root meaning.

What the **context** always shows is a God powerful enough to keep His promises when human strength has run out: to the barren, the aged, the bereaved.

Notice Naomi in Ruth 1:20-21. She uses this very name to say *the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me*. Scripture lets her say it. And the rest of the book shows the Almighty quietly working for her through Ruth and Boaz.

**In Christ:** The Greek equivalent, *Pantokrator*, “Almighty,” appears in Revelation nine times: “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God **Almighty**, who was and is and is to come” (Rev 4:8). The Almighty is the one who keeps His promise through the impossible birth and the empty tomb.
God introduced Himself as Almighty to a 99-year-old man waiting on a promise. What promise of God are you waiting on?
Naomi and Job both speak bitterly to Shaddai, and God doesn’t strike them down. What does that teach about honesty in prayer?

Be upfront that the meaning is debated; your group will trust you more for it. Don’t teach the “breasted one” as fact.

If someone loves the “God who is enough” idea: it’s a legitimate old Jewish interpretation and it’s true of God, but it isn’t certain etymology.

blocks.note: everlasting, forever; a long, unending stretch of time

blocks.text:
After making a treaty over a disputed well at **Beersheba**, Abraham plants a tamarisk tree and calls on “the name of the LORD, **the Everlasting God**” (Gen 21:33). Planting a slow-growing tree is itself an act of trust in the future: Abraham will not live to sit in its full shade, but the God he worships will still be there.

*Olam* means a very long time, “from age to age,” forever. Isaiah uses the same name to comfort exiles who think God has forgotten them: “The LORD is the **everlasting God**… He does not faint or grow weary” (Isa 40:28).

Psalm 90 is attributed to Moses, who lived a long life and saw a whole generation die in the wilderness. Against the shortness of human life he sets this: “from everlasting to everlasting you are God.”

**In Christ:** “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb 13:8). And what He gives is **eternal** life (John 17:3): not merely endless time, but life with the everlasting God.
Abraham planted a tree he wouldn’t see fully grown. What is something you can “plant” now for a future only God will see?
Isaiah 40 says the everlasting God doesn’t grow tired. Where are you tired right now?

Nice visual: bring a seedling or acorn.

Technical aside if asked: olam doesn’t always mean infinite (e.g. a servant “forever” in Exod 21:6 means for life). Context decides. When used of God it means without end.

blocks.note: to see; to see to it, to provide

blocks.text:
Genesis 22 is one of the hardest chapters in the Bible. God tells Abraham to offer Isaac, the son of the promise, on a mountain in the land of **Moriah**. On the way up, Isaac asks, “Where is the lamb?” Abraham answers, “God will **provide** for himself the lamb” (22:8).

God stops Abraham’s hand and provides a ram caught in a thicket. Abraham names the place **YHWH Yireh**, “the LORD will provide.”

The Hebrew verb is *ra’ah*, “**to see**.” So it literally means “the LORD will **see**,” in the sense of “see to it.” It is the same root as El Roi. The God who *sees* is the God who *sees to* our need.

**Where is Moriah?** 2 Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the temple “on **Mount Moriah**.” The place where God provided a substitute for Isaac became the place where sacrifices for sin were offered for a thousand years.

**In Christ:** John the Baptist points at Jesus: “Behold, **the Lamb of God**, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Abraham said God would provide the lamb; the ram was a substitute for one boy; the Lamb is the substitute for the world. And Paul echoes this chapter directly: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Rom 8:32; compare Gen 22:12, 16).
Abraham said “God will provide” before he saw the ram. What would it look like for you to say that before you see the answer?
God provided at the top of the mountain, not at the bottom. Why might God’s provision sometimes come only at the last moment?
How does Romans 8:32 turn this story into a promise for you?

Honest note: this is a place name Abraham gave the mountain, not a title God gave Himself. It is still a true confession about God.

Someone may ask how God could command this at all. Point to Heb 11:17-19 (Abraham reasoned God could raise the dead) and to the fact that God stopped it, and later did not spare His own Son. Don’t try to resolve it in two minutes; acknowledge it’s hard.

blocks.note: to heal, make whole, restore

blocks.text:
Three days after the Red Sea, Israel finds water at **Marah**, but it is bitter. The people grumble. God shows Moses a log, he throws it in, and the water becomes sweet. Then God says: “I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for **I am the LORD, your healer**” (Exod 15:26).

*Rapha* means to heal or make whole. In the Old Testament it is used of bodies, of land, of water, of a broken nation, and of the heart: “He **heals** the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Ps 147:3).

**An honest word.** This promise was given in the context of Israel’s covenant obedience, and it is not a guarantee that every believer will be physically healed whenever they ask. Paul prayed three times for his “thorn” to be removed and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Cor 12:7-9). He left his co-worker Trophimus sick (2 Tim 4:20). God does still heal, sometimes dramatically. But His deepest healing is of sin, and His full healing comes when He wipes every tear away (Rev 21:4).

**In Christ:** Jesus healed every kind of disease (Matt 4:23-24), and Isaiah’s great servant passage says, “with his wounds we are **healed**” (Isa 53:5), which Peter applies to sin: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree… by his wounds you have been healed” (1 Pet 2:24).
Israel complained at Marah only three days after a miracle. Why do we forget so quickly?
Where do you need God’s healing: body, heart, relationships, or something else?
How do you hold together “the LORD who heals” and Paul’s unhealed thorn?

Pastoral sensitivity: someone in the room may be ill, or may have lost someone they prayed for. Avoid any suggestion that lack of healing means lack of faith. Consider praying for anyone sick at the end of this section.

blocks.note: a banner, standard, signal pole raised high

blocks.text:
Israel’s first battle after leaving Egypt is against **Amalek**. Joshua fights in the valley; Moses stands on the hill with the staff of God raised. While his hands are up, Israel prevails; when they drop, Amalek prevails. Aaron and Hur hold up his arms until sunset.

Afterwards Moses builds an altar and names it **YHWH Nissi**, “the LORD is my banner.” A *nes* was a pole or standard raised high on a hill, something an army rallies around and looks to. Victory didn’t come from Joshua’s sword or Moses’ arms. It came from the LORD they lifted up.

**The same word shows up in a surprising place.** In Numbers 21, when the people are bitten by snakes, God tells Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a **pole**. That word is *nes*. Anyone who looked at it lived.

**In Christ:** Jesus says, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be **lifted up**, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14-15). Isaiah promised that the Root of Jesse would “stand as a **signal** (*nes*) for the peoples” (Isa 11:10). The cross is the banner: the thing raised high that we look to, rally around, and live by.
Moses needed Aaron and Hur to hold up his arms. Who holds up your arms? Whose arms are you holding up?
What do people today rally around as their “banner”? What does it mean to have the LORD as yours?

Exod 17:16 is a notoriously difficult verse (“a hand upon the throne of the LORD” vs. “a hand upon the banner of the LORD”). Not worth getting into unless asked.

Good visual: a flag. The *nes* in Num 21 → John 3:14 link usually gets an “oh!” from the group.

blocks.note: to make holy, set apart, consecrate

blocks.text:
God gave Israel the Sabbath as a sign “that you may know that **I, the LORD, sanctify you**” (Exod 31:13). The phrase is repeated through Leviticus’ holiness laws (Lev 20:8; 21:8; 22:32).

To **sanctify** is to make holy: to set something apart for God and make it fit for Him. Notice who does the work. God commands, “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev 11:44), and then says *He* is the one who makes them holy. The Sabbath, a day when Israel *stopped working*, was the sign of it.

**In Christ:** Jesus prays, “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth… for their sake I consecrate myself” (John 17:17-19). Hebrews says “we have been **sanctified** through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all,” and in the same breath that He is perfecting “those who are being sanctified” (Heb 10:10, 14). Holiness is both a gift already given and a work still going on, and both are God’s work: “He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (1 Thess 5:23-24).
Why do you think God made a day of rest the sign that He is the one who makes His people holy?
Do you tend to think of holiness as something you achieve, or something God does in you? How does this name change that?

The name is a phrase, not a formal title, but it is a recurring self-description of God in Leviticus. Pronunciation: meh-kah-DESH-kem (roughly).

Key contrast to draw: sanctification is not self-improvement.

blocks.note: peace, wholeness, completeness, well-being

blocks.text:
Israel is being crushed by Midian. **Gideon** is threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding. The angel of the LORD greets him as “mighty man of valour” and sends him to save Israel. When Gideon realises he has seen the angel of the LORD face to face, he is terrified he will die. The LORD says, “**Peace** be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die.”

Gideon builds an altar and calls it **YHWH Shalom**, “the LORD is peace.”

*Shalom* is much bigger than the absence of fighting. It means **wholeness**, everything as it should be: right with God, with others, within yourself, and in the world. Notice that Gideon’s first need for peace wasn’t peace with Midian; it was peace with God.

**In Christ:** Isaiah calls the coming child **Prince of Peace** (Isa 9:6). Paul says, “He himself **is our peace**” (Eph 2:14), and “since we have been justified by faith, we have **peace with God**” (Rom 5:1). Jesus says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives” (John 14:27). The peace Gideon received at an altar, we receive at the cross.
Gideon was afraid of meeting God. Why is peace *with* God the foundation for every other kind of peace?
Where in your life is shalom missing: what isn’t “whole” right now?
Close this section by reading the priestly blessing (Num 6:24-26) over the group.

blocks.note: hosts, armies; a great organised multitude

blocks.text:
**The LORD of hosts** is one of the most frequent titles for God in the Old Testament, around 285 times, especially in the prophets (Malachi uses it about two dozen times in four chapters). It first appears in 1 Samuel 1, in the story of **Hannah**, a woman who could not have children, praying in tears at Shiloh. She is the first person recorded addressing God by this name (1 Sam 1:11).

“Hosts” means **armies**. The title pictures God as commander of every force in heaven and earth: the angelic armies (1 Kgs 22:19), the stars He calls by name (Isa 40:26), and Israel’s own armies. When David faces Goliath he says, “I come to you in the name of **the LORD of hosts**” (1 Sam 17:45).

It’s worth noticing who uses this “military” name first: not a general, but a childless woman in anguish. The commander of heaven’s armies is approachable by the powerless.

Isaiah’s seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is **the LORD of hosts**; the whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isa 6:3).

**In Christ:** When Peter draws a sword in Gethsemane, Jesus says He could call on His Father for “more than twelve legions of angels” (Matt 26:53), and chooses not to. The Lord of hosts goes to the cross by choice. James even keeps the Hebrew word: the cries of the oppressed have reached the ears of “the Lord of **Sabaoth**” (Jas 5:4).
Hannah and David both used this name when facing something far bigger than them. What “giant” are you facing?
Psalm 46 repeats, “The LORD of hosts is with us.” Which do you need more: that He is powerful, or that He is with you?
Possible connection: Elisha’s servant in 2 Kgs 6:15-17, whose eyes are opened to see the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Great story for this name.

blocks.note: to shepherd, tend, feed, lead to pasture

blocks.text:
**“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”** David, who had been a shepherd boy himself, knew exactly what a shepherd does: he leads, feeds, protects, finds water, carries the weak, fights off predators, and brings the sheep home.

The picture of God as shepherd runs through the Old Testament. Dying Jacob speaks of “the God who has been **my shepherd** all my life long to this day” (Gen 48:15). Isaiah says, “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms” (Isa 40:11). And in Ezekiel 34, after Israel’s leaders have fed themselves instead of the flock, God says, “**I myself** will be the shepherd of my sheep… I will seek the lost” (Ezek 34:11-16).

**In Christ:** Jesus reads Ezekiel 34 and says, in effect, *that’s Me*. “**I am the good shepherd.** The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He is “the great shepherd of the sheep” (Heb 13:20), “the chief Shepherd” (1 Pet 5:4), and even in the end, “the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd” (Rev 7:17).
Psalm 23 moves from “He” to “You” at verse 4, in the valley. Why do you think the psalm becomes more personal in the dark?
Which shepherd action do you most need right now: leading, feeding, restoring, protecting, or bringing you home?

Point out the shift from “he” (vv. 1-3) to “you” (vv. 4-5) in Psalm 23. People love it.

Many will know Ps 23 by heart; consider saying it aloud together.

blocks.note: righteousness, rightness, what is just

blocks.text:
Jeremiah is prophesying as Judah’s last kings lead the nation to ruin. God promises that one day He will raise up for David “**a righteous Branch**,” a king who will reign wisely and do justice, “and this is the name by which he will be called: **The LORD is our righteousness**” (Jer 23:5-6).

**There is a sharp irony here.** The king on the throne when Jeremiah wrote was **Zedekiah**, whose name means “the LORD is my righteousness” (*Tsidqi-yahu*). He was weak, unfaithful and disobedient, and Jerusalem fell on his watch. God is saying: the man who wears that name now doesn’t live up to it, but I will send a King who truly *is* it.

Notice that the name is “the LORD is **our** righteousness.” Righteousness here is not just something the King has; it is something He gives His people. In 33:16 the same name is even given to Jerusalem: the people take on the righteousness of their King.

**In Christ:** This is the gospel in a name. “Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, **righteousness** and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor 1:30). “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become **the righteousness of God**” (2 Cor 5:21). Paul longs to be found in Christ “not having a righteousness of my own… but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Phil 3:9).
Zedekiah had a great name but didn’t live it. Where do you see a gap between the name “Christian” and how you live?
What is the difference between trying to be righteous and receiving righteousness? How does it change how you feel when you fail?

The Zedekiah irony is the hook; slow down for it. Most commentators note it.

Good place to clearly explain justification by faith if you have people who aren’t believers in the room.

blocks.note: there; in that place

blocks.text:
The book of Ezekiel ends with a vision of a restored city, and its very last words give the city a new name: “**The LORD is there**” (Ezek 48:35).

To feel how powerful that is, you have to know the middle of the book. In chapters 10-11, Ezekiel watches **the glory of the LORD leave the temple**, pause at the threshold, move to the east gate, and finally depart to the mountain east of the city. Because of Israel’s sin, God’s presence leaves. Jerusalem falls soon after.

Then in chapter 43, Ezekiel sees **the glory return** from the east and fill the temple again. The book that watched God leave ends with a city whose name is the promise that He will never leave again.

**In Christ:** “The Word became flesh and **dwelt** (literally *tabernacled*) among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). His name is **Immanuel**, God with us (Matt 1:23), and His last promise in Matthew is, “I am **with you** always” (Matt 28:20).

The Bible ends where Ezekiel ends: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them” (Rev 21:3), in a city that needs no temple and no sun, “for the glory of God gives it light” (Rev 21:22-23).
Have you ever felt like God’s presence had left? What helped, or what would help?
If someone looked at your home, your church, or your life, what would make them say “the LORD is there”?
Visual idea: trace the glory’s exit path in Ezek 10-11 on a simple temple sketch, then its return in 43. Then jump to John 1:14 and Rev 21:3. This section can be the emotional climax of the lesson.

blocks.note: jealous, zealous; used only of God

blocks.text:
This name makes people uncomfortable, so it’s worth facing head-on. In the Ten Commandments God says, “You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am **a jealous God**” (Exod 20:5). And in Exodus 34:14: “the LORD, whose **name is Jealous**, is a jealous God.”

In human beings, jealousy is often petty and insecure. That isn’t this. The Hebrew word *qanna* is used only of God, and it describes the **rightful, protective zeal** of a husband for his wife. God has bound Himself to His people in a covenant like a marriage. When they run after idols, the Bible calls it adultery (Hos 1-3; Ezek 16). A husband who didn’t care if his wife left him wouldn’t be more loving; he’d be indifferent.

God’s jealousy is not jealousy *of* anyone; nothing threatens Him. It is jealousy *for* someone: for His people, because idols cannot save them and will only destroy them.

**In Christ:** Paul says to the Corinthians, “I feel a **divine jealousy** for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor 11:2). The church is the bride of Christ (Eph 5:25-27), and He loved her enough to give Himself up for her.
How is God’s jealousy different from the jealousy we usually see in people?
What modern “idols” compete for your heart? What would it look like to be faithful to God in that area?

Expect pushback; that’s good. Acknowledge the discomfort first, then explain the marriage picture. Hosea is the best illustration.

James 4:5 is sometimes cited here but its translation is genuinely disputed; avoid leaning on it.

blocks.note: living, alive

blocks.text:
As Israel stands at the Jordan about to enter Canaan, Joshua says, “Here is how you shall know that **the living God** is among you”: the river will stop and they will cross on dry ground (Josh 3:10).

The phrase “the living God” is always set against **dead idols**: gods made of wood and gold that “have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see” (Ps 115:4-8). The living God speaks, acts, hears, rescues and judges. David is outraged that Goliath would “defy the armies of **the living God**” (1 Sam 17:26). The psalmist thirsts for Him: “My soul thirsts for God, for **the living God**” (Ps 42:2).

**In Christ:** Peter’s great confession is, “You are the Christ, the Son of **the living God**” (Matt 16:16). The Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve **the living and true God**” (1 Thess 1:9). And the risen Jesus says, “I am **the living one**. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore” (Rev 1:18).

One sober note: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb 10:31). A living God is not tame.
What is the difference between serving a living God and serving an idol? What do idols demand that God doesn’t, and vice versa?
Psalm 42 describes thirst for the living God. When have you felt that thirst?
Pair with Psalm 115:4-8, the satire on idols. Ask: “we become like what we worship” (v. 8) — what does that mean?

blocks.note: to be firm, reliable, trustworthy. The root behind “faithful,” “truth” and “amen”

blocks.text:
In his final song, Moses calls God “The Rock, his work is perfect… **a God of faithfulness** (*El Emunah*) and without iniquity, just and upright is he” (Deut 32:4). Earlier he told Israel, “Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, **the faithful God** who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him… to a thousand generations” (Deut 7:9).

The Hebrew root *’aman* means firm, solid, reliable, something you can lean your weight on. It is where we get the word **Amen**: “it is firm,” “it is true.” When you say Amen, you are using the same root as God’s faithfulness.

The most famous line about God’s faithfulness comes from the bleakest book in the Bible. Jerusalem has been destroyed, and in the middle of Lamentations the poet says, “His mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; **great is your faithfulness**” (Lam 3:22-23).

**In Christ:** “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” (1 Cor 1:9). “If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim 2:13). “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). And when Jesus returns, He rides a white horse and is called **Faithful and True** (Rev 19:11). All God’s promises find their “Yes” in Him, “that is why it is through him that we utter our **Amen**” (2 Cor 1:20).
“Great is your faithfulness” was written among ruins. Why does that make it more believable, not less?
Where have you seen God’s faithfulness in your own story? Take a moment to share one example.

Strictly, Deut 32:4 uses emunah (H0530) and Deut 7:9 uses ne’eman (H0539); same root. The word card shows the root.

Great moment for testimonies. Give people a minute to think before asking.

sections.title: Ancient of Days
sections.subtitle: The eternal Judge on the throne

blocks.note: ancient, advanced in age (Aramaic)

blocks.text:
In Daniel 7, after a vision of four terrifying beasts (empires that rise and devour), Daniel sees thrones set in place and **the Ancient of Days** take His seat. His clothing is white as snow, His hair like pure wool, His throne fiery flames. The court sits in judgment, and the beasts lose their power.

Then comes the key moment: “one like **a son of man**” comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given “dominion and glory and a kingdom… an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away” (Dan 7:13-14).

The name pictures God as the eternal, all-wise Judge who outlasts every empire. Kingdoms that seem unstoppable are, before Him, just beasts waiting for the verdict.

**In Christ:** At His trial, when the high priest asks if He is the Christ, Jesus answers, “I am, and you will see **the Son of Man** seated at the right hand of Power, and **coming with the clouds of heaven**” (Mark 14:61-62), quoting Daniel 7. The high priest tears his robes.

And in Revelation 1:13-14, John sees the risen Jesus: “one like a son of man… The hairs of his head were **white, like white wool, like snow**.” The description of the Ancient of Days is given to Jesus. The Son shares the Father’s eternal glory.
Daniel saw the empires of his day as beasts. What “beasts” feel powerful today, and how does this vision put them in perspective?
Why do you think Revelation 1 describes Jesus with the features of the Ancient of Days?

Daniel 7 is in Aramaic, not Hebrew (Dan 2:4b–7:28), which is why this word looks different.

Watch time: this is a rich passage and easy to over-run. The key line is Mark 14:62.

sections.title: Calling on His name
sections.subtitle: What we do with what we’ve learned

blocks.text:
We’ve walked through more than twenty names. Put them side by side and they tell a story: the **Creator** (Elohim) who is **Most High** (El Elyon) and **Almighty** (El Shaddai) is also the God who **sees** a runaway slave (El Roi), **provides** a lamb (Yireh), **heals** (Rapha), **fights** for us (Nissi, Sabaoth), **makes us holy** (Mekoddishkem), gives **peace** (Shalom), **shepherds** us (Rohi), becomes our **righteousness** (Tsidkenu), and promises to be **there** forever (Shammah).

And almost every one of those names finds its fullest meaning in **Jesus**, whose own name means “the LORD saves.” He is the Lamb provided, the Banner lifted up, our Peace, the Good Shepherd, our Righteousness, God with us.

In John 17, Jesus sums up His whole ministry by saying, “I have **manifested your name**,” and “I made known to them **your name**, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them.” Knowing God’s name is never just information. It is meant to lead to love and trust.

So the right response is the one the Bible keeps modelling: **call on His name.** Pray using these names. When you are afraid, pray to El Roi. When you are in need, to YHWH Yireh. When you fail, to YHWH Tsidkenu.
Which name of God meant the most to you in this study? Why?
Pick one name to pray with every day this week. Which one, and what situation will you bring to it?
Jesus said He made God’s name known “that the love with which you have loved me may be in them.” How does knowing God’s names lead to love?

Close by praying through several names aloud, or invite people to pray a one-sentence prayer using a name that spoke to them.

Coming next: Part 2, the names and titles of Jesus; Part 3, the Holy Spirit.
